A

Next month, a chess player named Timur Gareyev will take on nearly 50 opponents at once. But that is not the hard part. While his challengers will play the games as normal, Gareyev himself will be blindfolded. Even by world record standards, it sets a high bar for human performance. The 28-year-old already stands out in the rarefied world of blindfold chess. He has a fondness for bright clothes and unusual hairstyles, and he gets his kicks from the adventure sport of BASE jumping. He has already proved himself a strong chess player, too. In a 10-hour chess marathon in 2013, Gareyev played 33 games in his head simultaneously. He won 29 and lost none. The skill has become his brand: he calls himself the Blindfold King.

B

But Gareyev’s prowess has drawn interest from beyond the chess-playing community. In the hope of understanding how he and others like him can perform such mental feats, researchers at the University of California in Los Angeles (UCLA) called him in for tests. They now have their first results. ‘The ability to play a game of chess with your eyes closed is not a far reach for most accomplished player,’ said Jesse Rissman, who runs a memory lab at UCLA. ‘But the thing that’s so remarkable about Timur and a few other individuals is the number of games they can keep active at once. To me it is simply astonishing.’

C

Gareyev learned to play chess in his native Uzbekistan when he was six years old. Tutored by his grandfather, he entered his first tournament aged eight and soon became obsessed with competitions. At 16, he was crowned Asia’s youngest ever chess grandmaster. He moved to the US soon after, and as a student helped his university win its first national chess championship. In 2013, Gareyev was ranked the third best chess player in the US.

D

To the uninitiated, blindfold chess seems to call for superhuman skill. But displays of the feat go back centuries. The first recorded game in Europe was played in 13th-century Florence. In 1947, the Argentinian grandmaster Miguel Najdorf played 45 simultaneous games in his mind, winning 39 in the 24-hour session.

E

Accomplished players can develop the skill of playing blind even without realising it. The nature of the game is to run through possible moves in the mind to see how they play out. From this, regular players develop a memory for the patterns the pieces make, the defences and attacks. ‘You recreate it in your mind,’ said Gareyev. ‘A lot of players are capable of doing what I’m doing.’ The real mental challenge comes from playing multiple games at once in the head. Not only must the positions of each piece on every board be memorised, they must be recalled faithfully when needed, updated with each player’s moves, and then reliably stored again, so the brain can move on to the next board. First moves can be tough to remember because they are fairly uninteresting. But the ends of games are taxing too, as exhaustion sets in. When Gareyev is tired, his recall can get patchy. He sometimes makes moves based on only a fragmented memory of the pieces’ positions.

F

The scientists first had Gareyev perform some standard memory tests. These assessed his ability to hold numbers, pictures and words in mind. One classic test measures how many numbers a person can repeat, both forwards and backwards, soon after hearing them. Most people manage about seven. ‘He was not exceptional on any of these standard tests,’ said Rissman. ‘We didn’t find anything other than playing chess that he seems to be supremely gifted at.’ But next came the brain scans. With Gareyev lying down in the machine, Rissman looked at how well connected the various regions of the chess player’s brain were. Though the results are tentative and as yet unpublished, the scans found much greater than average communication between parts of Gareyev’s brain that make up what is called the frontoparietal control network. Of 63 people scanned alongside the chess player, only one or two scored more highly on the measure. ‘You use this network in almost any complex task. It helps you to allocate attention, keep rules in mind, and work out whether you should be responding or not,’ said Rissman.

G

It was not the only hint of something special in Gareyev’s brain. The scans also suggest that Gareyev’s visual network is more highly connected to other brain parts than usual. Initial results suggest that the areas of his brain that process visual images – such as chess boards – may have stronger links to other brain regions, and so be more powerful than normal. While the analyses are not finalised yet, they may hold the first clues to Gareyev’s extraordinary ability.

H

For the world record attempt, Gareyev hopes to play 47 blindfold games at once in about 16 hours. He will need to win 80% to claim the title. ‘I don’t worry too much about the winning percentage, that’s never been an issue for me,’ he said. ‘The most important part of blindfold chess for me is that I have found the one thing that I can fully dedicate myself to. I miss having an obsession.’

### READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on **Questions** **1-13** which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

## The coconut palm

For millennia, the coconut has been central to the lives of Polynesian and Asian peoples. In the western world, on the other hand, coconuts have always been exotic and unusual, sometimes rare. The Italian merchant traveller Marco Polo apparently saw coconuts in South Asia in the late 13th century, and among the mid-14th-century travel writings of Sir John Mandeville there is mention of ‘great Notes of Ynde’ (great Nuts of India). Today, images of palm-fringed tropical beaches are clichés in the west to sell holidays, chocolate bars, fizzy drinks and even romance.

Typically, we envisage coconuts as brown cannonballs that, when opened, provide sweet white flesh. But we see only part of the fruit and none of the plant from which they come. The coconut palm has a smooth, slender, grey trunk, up to 30 metres tall. This is an important source of timber for building houses, and is increasingly being used as a replacement for endangered hardwoods in the furniture construction industry. The trunk is surmounted by a rosette of leaves, each of which may be up to six metres long. The leaves have hard veins in their centres which, in many parts of the world, are used as brushes after the green part of the leaf has been stripped away. Immature coconut flowers are tightly clustered together among the leaves at the top of the trunk. The flower stems may be tapped for their sap to produce a drink, and the sap can also be reduced by boiling to produce a type of sugar used for cooking.

Coconut palms produce as many as seventy fruits per year, weighing more than a kilogram each. The wall of the fruit has three layers: a waterproof outer layer, a fibrous middle layer and a hard, inner layer. The thick fibrous middle layer produces coconut fibre, ‘coir’, which has numerous uses and is particularly important in manufacturing ropes. The woody innermost layer, the shell, with its three prominent ‘eyes’, surrounds the seed. An important product obtained from the shell is charcoal, which is widely used in various industries as well as in the home as a cooking fuel. When broken in half, the shells are also used as bowls in many parts of Asia.

Inside the shell are the nutrients (endosperm) needed by the developing seed. Initially, the endosperm is a sweetish liquid, coconut water, which is enjoyed as a drink, but also provides the hormones which encourage other plants to grow more rapidly and produce higher yields. As the fruit matures, the coconut water gradually solidifies to form the brilliant white, fat-rich, edible flesh or meat. Dried coconut flesh, ‘copra’, is made into coconut oil and coconut milk, which are widely used in cooking in different parts of the world, as well as in cosmetics. A derivative of coconut fat, glycerine, acquired strategic importance in a quite different sphere, as Alfred Nobel introduced the world to his nitroglycerine-based invention: dynamite.

Their biology would appear to make coconuts the great maritime voyagers and coastal colonizers of the plant world. The large, energy-rich fruits are able to float in water and tolerate salt, but cannot remain viable indefinitely; studies suggest after about 110 days at sea they are no longer able to germinate. Literally cast onto desert island shores, with little more than sand to grow in and exposed to the full glare of the tropical sun, coconut seeds are able to germinate and root. The air pocket in the seed, created as the endosperm solidifies, protects the embryo. In addition, the fibrous fruit wall that helped it to float during the voyage stores moisture that can be taken up by the roots of the coconut seedling as it starts to grow.

There have been centuries of academic debate over the origins of the coconut. There were no coconut palms in West Africa, the Caribbean or the east coast of the Americans before the voyages of the European explorers Vasco da Gama and Columbus in the late 15th and early 16th centuries. 16th century trade and human migration patterns reveal that Arab traders and European sailors are likely to have moved coconuts from South and Southeast Asia to Africa and then across the Atlantic to the east coast of America. But the origin of coconuts discovered along the west coast of America by 16th century sailors has been the subject of centuries of discussion. Two diametrically opposed origins have been proposed: that they came from Asia, or that they were native to America. Both suggestions have problems. In Asia, there is a large degree of coconut diversity and evidence of millennia of human use – but there are no relatives growing in the wild. In America, there are close coconut relatives, but no evidence that coconuts are indigenous. These problems have led to the intriguing suggestion that coconuts originated on coral islands in the Pacific and were dispersed from there.

#### Questions 9-13 Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1? *In boxes **9-13** on your answer sheet, write* **TRUE** if the statement agrees with the information **FALSE** if the statement contradicts the information **NOT GIVEN** if there is no information on this **9** Coconut seeds need shade in order to germinate. **10** Coconuts were probably transported to Asia from America in the 16 th century. **11** Coconuts found on the west coast of America were a different type from those found on the east coast. **12** All the coconuts found in Asia are cultivated varieties. **13** Coconuts are cultivated in different ways in America and the Pacific. ### READING PASSAGE 2 You should spend about 20 minutes on **Questions 14-26** which are based on Reading Passage 2 below. ## How baby talk gives infant brains a boost **A** The typical way of talking to a baby – high-pitched, exaggerated and repetitious – is a source of fascination for linguists who hope to understand how ‘baby talk’ impacts on learning. Most babies start developing their hearing while still in the womb, prompting some hopeful parents to play classical music to their pregnant bellies. Some research even suggests that infants are listening to adult speech as early as 10 weeks before being born, gathering the basic building blocks of their family’s native tongue. **B** Early language exposure seems to have benefits to the brain – for instance, studies suggest that babies raised in bilingual homes are better at learning how to mentally prioritize information. So how does the sweet if sometimes absurd sound of infant-directed speech influence a baby’s development? Here are some recent studies that explore the science behind baby talk. **C** Fathers don’t use baby talk as often or in the same ways as mothers – and that’s perfectly OK, according to a new study. Mark VanDam of Washington State University at Spokane and colleagues equipped parents with recording devices and speech-recognition software to study the way they interacted with their youngsters during a normal day. ‘We found that moms do exactly what you’d expect and what’s been described many times over,’ VanDam explains. ‘But we found that dads aren’t doing the same thing. Dads didn’t raise their pitch or fundamental frequency when they talked to kids.’ Their role may be rooted in what is called the bridge hypothesis, which dates back to 1975. It suggests that fathers use less familial language to provide their children with a bridge to the kind of speech they’ll hear in public. ‘The idea is that a kid gets to practice a certain kind of speech with mom and another kind of speech with dad, so the kid then has a wider repertoire of kinds of speech to practice,’ says VanDam. **D** Scientists from the University of Washington and the University of Connecticut collected thousands of 30-second conversations between parents and their babies, fitting 26 children with audio-recording vests that captured language and sound during a typical eight-hour day. The study found that the more baby talk parents used, the more their youngsters began to babble. And when researchers saw the same babies at age two, they found that frequent baby talk had dramatically boosted vocabulary, regardless of socioeconomic status. ‘Those children who listened to a lot of baby talk were talking more than the babies that listened to more adult talk or standard speech,’ says Nairán Ramirez-Esparza of the University of Connecticut. ‘We also found that it really matters whether you use baby talk in a one-on-one context,’ she adds. ‘The more parents use baby talk one-on-one, the more babies babble, and the more they babble, the more words they produce later in life.’ **E** Another study suggests that parents might want to pair their youngsters up so they can babble more with their own kind. Researchers from McGill University and Université du Québec à Montréal found that babies seem to like listening to each other rather than to adults – which may be why baby talk is such a universal tool among parents. They played repeating vowel sounds made by a special synthesizing device that mimicked sounds made by either an adult woman or another baby. This way, only the impact of the auditory cues was observed. The team then measured how long each type of sound held the infants’ attention. They found that the ‘infant’ sounds held babies’ attention nearly 40 percent longer. The baby noises also induced more reactions in the listening infants, like smiling or lip moving, which approximates sound making. The team theorizes that this attraction to other infant sounds could help launch the learning process that leads to speech. ‘It may be some property of the sound that is just drawing their attention,’ says study co-author Linda Polka. ‘Or maybe they are really interested in that particular type of sound because they are starting to focus on their own ability to make sounds. We are speculating here but it might catch their attention because they recognize it as a sound they could possibly make.’ **F** In a study published in *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, a total of 57 babies from two slightly different age groups – seven months and eleven and a half months – were played a number of syllables from both their native language (English) and a non-native tongue (Spanish). The infants were placed in a brain-activation scanner that recorded activity in a brain region known to guide the motor movements that produce speech. The results suggest that listening to baby talk prompts infant brains to start practicing their language skills. ‘Finding activation in motor areas the baby brain is engaged in trying to talk back right from the start, and suggests that seven-month-olds’ brains are already trying to figure out how to make interesting finding was that while the seven-month-olds responded to all speech sounds regardless of language, the brains of the older infants worked harder at the motor activations of non-native sounds compared to native sounds. The study may have also uncovered a process by which babies recognize differences between their native language and other tongues. #### Questions 14-17 Look at the following ideas (Questions **14-17**) and the list of researchers below. passage.content:
The notion of "de-extinction," or biological resurrection, has transitioned from the realm of science fiction to a tangible, albeit controversial, scientific pursuit. The primary candidate for this procedure is the Woolly Mammoth. Scientists are currently employing CRISPR technology to splice mammoth DNA into the genome of the Asian elephant, its closest living relative. The objective is not merely to create a biological curiosity but to restore the "Mammoth Steppe" ecosystem in the Arctic.

Proponents argue that reintroducing these mega-herbivores could combat climate change. By trampling the snow and knocking down trees, mammoths would expose the ground to freezing Arctic air, thereby preserving the permafrost. **It** acts as a massive carbon sink; if it melts, it releases catastrophic amounts of methane. Thus, the mammoth is envisioned as a geo-engineering tool, a hairy bulwark against global warming.

However, ethical objections abound. **Critics question the morality of bringing a social, intelligent animal into into today's world, which lacks the climate, ecosystem, and social structures the species once depended on, potentially subjecting it to a lonely existence in a zoo-like environment.** Furthermore, conservationists worry that the colossal funding required for de-extinction could divert resources from saving extant species that are currently teetering on the brink of oblivion. The fear is that we might trade the existence of the living for the resurrection of the dead.

Ultimately, the debate transcends biology. It forces us to confront our role as stewards of the planet. Are we correcting a past mistake the likely human-induced extinction of the mammoth or are we indulging in scientific hubris? As technology advances, the line between what we "can" do and what we "should" do becomes increasingly blurred, leaving us to navigate a moral landscape as treacherous as the melting permafrost itself.

passage.content:
In the bustling alleyways of rapidly developing nations, a silent social contract exists. It is played out over bowls of noodles and cups of strong coffee, where cash changes hands without the whir of a receipt printer. This is the shadow economy, a vast, **nebulous** zone where tax evasion is not viewed as theft, but as a pragmatic adjustment to reality. For many, under-declaring income is not an act of malice; it is a normalized defense mechanism against a system perceived as inefficient or corrupt.

The psychology behind this normalization is complex. [I] **It** stems from a concept known as "fiscal exchange theory," which posits that tax compliance is directly linked to the perceived quality of public services. When citizens see potholed roads, underfunded schools, and official extravagance, the moral obligation to pay taxes dissolves. It is replaced by a cynical rationality: "Why should I feed a system that does not feed me?" Consequently, fraud becomes a socially acceptable rebellion, a way for the "little guy" to level the playing field against a monolithic state.

However, the aggregate effect of this individual rationality is collectively disastrous. [II] It creates a vicious cycle: low tax revenue leads to poor public services, which in turn fuels further evasion. Moreover, it distorts market competition. **Honest businesses that comply with regulations find themselves undercut by competitors who treat tax evasion as a margin of profit.** This creates an environment where integrity is penalized and deceit is rewarded, fundamentally warping the economic structure.

Addressing this requires more than just punitive measures; it demands a restoration of the social contract. Governments often resort to technological crackdowns, forcing digital payments to track transactions. [III] Without a corresponding increase in transparency and accountability, such measures are viewed as oppressive rather than corrective. True normalization of tax compliance will only occur when the state is viewed not as a predator, but as a partner. Until the populace believes that their contribution serves the common good rather than private pockets, the shadow economy will remain an enduring, if not dominant, feature of the landscape. [IV]

The psychology of investment is shaped by a range of cognitive biases that influence how people make financial decisions. Investors often assume they act rationally; however, in reality, they are frequently influenced by collective behaviour rather than independent analysis. This tendency, widely observed across financial markets, (30)______. As a result, the fear of missing out (FOMO) can drive speculative market bubbles. Investors may then question whether an asset is genuinely valuable, or (31)______.

Be that as it may, experienced investors recognise that volatility is an inherent feature of the market rather than a sign of immediate danger. While inexperienced traders often panic at the first indication of a downturn, seasoned participants tend to interpret such moments as potential opportunities. (32)______. There is substantial evidence indicating that emotional discipline, rather than sheer intellectual ability, plays a decisive role in long-term investment success. (34)______, the intelligent investor can navigate market uncertainty without giving in to irrational fear.

sections.instructionText: Read the following passage about Patterns That Guide Professional Growth and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 23 to 30.
sections.name: Section 5

passage.content:
Career trajectories rarely follow linear paths in today's dynamic workplace. Instead, they resemble constellations—unique patterns of pivotal experiences, skill acquisition, and professional relationships that collectively shape one's journey. These configurations often emerge organically, yet discerning professionals actively cultivate their career constellations, strategically forging connections between seemingly disparate experiences. Unlike traditional career ladders, constellations accommodate lateral moves, temporary setbacks, and unexpected opportunities that ultimately enhance one's professional versatility.

Different constellation archetypes manifest across industries. The "specialist" constellation features closely clustered experiences, deepening their expertise in a singular domain. Conversely, the "generalist" pattern displays widely dispersed points demonstrating breadth across multiple sectors. The "entrepreneur" constellation often shows cyclical patterns of venture creation, while the "corporate climber" typically exhibits an upward trajectory within organizational hierarchies.

Research indicates that approximately 65% of professionals unknowingly replicate established constellation patterns, while others deliberately craft unprecedented configurations aligned with emerging market demands. To leverage your constellation effectively, begin by mapping significant professional milestones and identifying recurring themes. This retrospective analysis often reveals latent aptitudes and propensities that might otherwise remain obscured. Subsequently, assess which connections between experiences have expedited your growth and which gaps warrant attention. Mentors prove invaluable during this process, offering nuanced perspectives on your constellation's distinctive features. Their guidance helps circumvent common pitfalls while illuminating potential pathways that align with your intrinsic motivations.

The paradigm shift toward portfolio careers has transformed how constellations form in contemporary workplaces. Today's professionals increasingly amalgamate full-time positions with side projects, continuous learning initiatives, and community endeavors. This multidimensional approach creates resilient constellations that weather industry disruptions. Furthermore, digital platforms now enable professionals to showcase their constellations beyond traditional resumes, highlighting the narrative coherence underlying seemingly divergent experiences. Those who master this holistic representation position themselves advantageously in an economy that increasingly values adaptability over linear advancement.

sections.instructionText: Read the following passage about the Distributed AI Systems Monitoring Earth's Vital Signs and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 31 to 40.
sections.name: Section 6

passage.content:
In the race against accelerating climate degradation, researchers have adopted a no holds barred approach to environmental monitoring. Climate Intelligence Networks—sophisticated mesh systems of interconnected sensors, satellites, and computational nodes—now function as Earth's diagnostic apparatus. [I] These decentralized frameworks autonomously collect, analyze, and disseminate critical ecological data with unprecedented granularity. Unlike conventional monitoring stations, which provide merely fragmented snapshots, these networks generate comprehensive, real-time visualizations of planetary health indicators, from atmospheric composition to oceanic thermal anomalies. The integration of quantum computing algorithms further amplifies their predictive capabilities, enabling forecasting models with 85% greater accuracy than previous-generation systems.

The operational architecture of these networks leverages edge computing, whereby data processing occurs proximal to collection points rather than centralized facilities. [II] This topology minimizes latency while maximizing responsiveness to emergent phenomena. Biomimetic sensors—devices engineered to emulate natural sensing mechanisms—constitute the network's peripheral nervous system. These imperceptible nodes, often no larger than pollen grains, can be dispersed across inaccessible terrain via drone deployment. Upon activation, they establish self-organizing neural networks, recalibrating autonomously to accommodate environmental perturbations. This distributed intelligence paradigm ensures resilience against localized disruptions, maintaining functionality despite component attrition.

[III] In tropical rainforests, arboreal sensor arrays detect minute shifts in canopy density and biodiversity metrics, flagging deforestation activities days before satellite verification. Similarly, deep-ocean monitoring clusters track acidification gradients and thermal stratification with millimeter precision, revolutionizing coral reef preservation strategies. Agricultural applications include soil moisture optimization systems that have reduced water consumption by 37% across pilot regions while maintaining yield integrity. Perhaps most remarkably, urban deployments interface with municipal infrastructure, orchestrating energy distribution based on microclimate fluctuations and anthropogenic emissions.

Ethical considerations inevitably accompany this technological proliferation. Questions regarding data sovereignty persist, particularly concerning indigenous territories where installation often precedes consultation. Privacy advocates highlight potential surveillance applications, while cybersecurity experts warn of vulnerabilities that could permit ecological data manipulation. Despite these legitimate concerns, the consensus among climatologists suggests these systems represent our most sophisticated mechanism for environmental stewardship. [IV] As computational power continues its exponential trajectory, these networks will likely evolve from passive monitoring tools into active planetary maintenance systems, potentially orchestrating large-scale carbon sequestration and atmospheric regulation initiatives.

sections.instructionText: V. GATEWAYS TO EFFECTIVE WORK HABITS Read the following passage about Gateways to Effective Work Habits and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 23 to 30.
sections.name: V. GATEWAYS TO EFFECTIVE WORK HABITS

passage.content:
In today's hyperconnected workplace, productivity portals serve as indispensable nexuses that streamline disparate workflows into cohesive systems. These digital ecosystems transcend conventional task management by amalgamating scheduling, communication, and project oversight into unified interfaces that mitigate cognitive fragmentation. While the proliferation of digital tools has revolutionized knowledge work, the judicious implementation of productivity frameworks remains paramount. Studies indicate that professionals who leverage integrated productivity systems demonstrate a 37% reduction in task-switching penalties, thereby curtailing the deleterious effects of attention **residue**.

The architecture of effective productivity portals hinges on their capacity to harmonize functionality with intuitive design. Time-blocking applications, which partition the workday into dedicated segments, foster deep concentration by establishing temporal boundaries. Concurrently, digital Kanban systems facilitate visual workflow management, enabling teams to circumnavigate bottlenecks through instantaneous progress visualization. These methodologies, when coupled with automated reminder systems, cultivate accountability while obviating the need for perpetual **vigilance**.

The synergy between these components engenders a self-reinforcing cycle of productivity enhancement. The ramifications of implementing sophisticated productivity frameworks extend beyond mere efficiency gains. Organizations that espouse comprehensive digital ecosystems report substantial improvements in employee satisfaction metrics, primarily attributed to the autonomy and clarity these systems confer. **Moreover, the asynchronous nature of many productivity tools has rendered geographical constraints increasingly obsolete, fostering unprecedented collaboration across temporal zones.** This democratization of workflow management has precipitated a paradigm shift wherein individual contributors can orchestrate their productivity rhythms in accordance with their cognitive chronotypes.

Selecting appropriate productivity portals necessitates discernment regarding one's cognitive proclivities and workflow peculiarities. The allure of feature-rich applications often overshadows the virtue of simplicity, potentially exacerbating the very complexities they purport to resolve. Consequently, professionals should prioritize systems that complement **their** existing work patterns rather than mandate wholesale behavioral transformations. Furthermore, incremental integration proves more sustainable than abrupt overhauls, as it facilitates gradual adaptation. The ultimate efficacy of any productivity framework resides not in its technological sophistication but in its alignment with human cognitive architecture.

sections.instructionText: VI. THE REPRESENTATION REVOLUTION Read the following passage about the Representation Revolution and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 31 to 40.
sections.name: VI. THE REPRESENTATION REVOLUTION

passage.content:
For decades, indigenous storytellers have **fallen on hard times** when attempting to penetrate mainstream media ecosystems. Their narratives, rich with cultural nuance and historical significance, were systematically marginalized, deemed commercially unviable, or appropriated without proper attribution. This exclusion not only deprived indigenous communities of platforms for self-representation but also perpetuated harmful stereotypes that permeated collective consciousness. [I] Recently, however, a paradigm shift has emerged, with indigenous creators leveraging digital democratization to circumvent traditional gatekeepers and assert their authentic perspectives in unprecedented ways.

The impediments to indigenous representation extend beyond mere visibility issues to encompass structural inequities embedded within media institutions. Financing remains a formidable barrier, with indigenous productions receiving disproportionately limited investment compared to conventional content. Furthermore, the persistent demand for indigenous stories to conform to **preconceived** notions—often centered around trauma narratives or mystical stereotypes—undermines creative autonomy. [II] When representation does occur, it frequently manifests as tokenistic inclusion rather than meaningful engagement with indigenous worldviews and contemporary realities.

Despite these obstacles, indigenous creators have orchestrated remarkable breakthroughs across various platforms. [III] Films such as "Reservation Dogs" and "Rutherford Falls" have demonstrated that Indigenous narratives can achieve both critical acclaim and commercial success while maintaining cultural integrity. Social media platforms have similarly fostered indigenous content creators who cultivate substantial followings by offering unfiltered glimpses into **their** communities, effectively circumventing mainstream media's historical gatekeeping mechanisms.

The trajectory of indigenous representation signals a transformative period in media evolution, yet substantial work remains. [IV] Educational institutions must prioritize indigenous media literacy to cultivate discerning audiences. **Media conglomerates should implement structural reforms, including indigenous leadership in decision-making positions and equitable resource allocation.** Most crucially, this representation revolution must extend beyond tokenistic diversity initiatives to embrace genuine plurality of perspectives. As indigenous voices increasingly permeate mainstream channels, they not only reclaim narrative sovereignty but also enrich the global cultural landscape with previously suppressed knowledge systems and artistic traditions.

passage.content:
Key Points to Remember on Traffic Rules in England

Below are some key points you need to remember when you travel in England.

The general rule of keeping left: When you are driving on a road which is a two-way road, you need to allow the traffic from the opposite direction to pass from your right side. Similarly, all the vehicles in your lane also need to be given the right side to **overtake**.

When you turn: When you are taking a turn, always keep to your turning side, meaning when turning right, get to the right side of the road and do the same when turning to the left.

Do not park: Surely, you want to park your vehicle as fast as you can, but that doesn't mean you leave your car on the side of the road. Find the parking near your building and park it there. If parking is not available, make sure you are not parking near the bus stand, school, or hospital entrance.

Do not drive: When you are going on a one-way road, you cannot reverse your vehicle.

Use indicators: When you are changing lanes, overtaking the other car, or taking a turn, always use turn signals or indicators to make fellow drivers know about your manoeuvre.

Do not cross the stop line: At the traffic signal, when you get to stop your vehicle due to a red signal, make sure you are not keeping your car on the stop line or on the pedestrian crossing.

Below are some key points you need to remember when you travel in England.

The general rule of keeping left: When you are driving on a road which is a two-way road, you need to allow the traffic from the opposite direction to pass from your right side. Similarly, all the vehicles in your lane also need to be given the right side to **overtake**.

When you turn: When you are taking a turn, always keep to your turning side, meaning when turning right, get to the right side of the road and do the same when turning to the left.

Do not park: Surely, you want to park your vehicle as fast as you can, but that doesn't mean you leave your car on the side of the road. Find the parking near your building and park it there. If parking is not available, make sure you are not parking near the bus stand, school, or hospital entrance.

Do not drive: When you are going on a one-way road, you cannot reverse your vehicle.

Use indicators: When you are changing lanes, overtaking the other car, or taking a turn, always use turn signals or indicators to make fellow drivers know about your manoeuvre.

Do not cross the stop line: At the traffic signal, when you get to stop your vehicle due to a red signal, make sure you are not keeping your car on the stop line or on the pedestrian crossing.

sections.passageContent:
English has become a global language, and Europe is no exception. While it's not the native tongue of most Europeans, English plays an important role in education business, and international communication. But the English spoken in Europe isn't monolithic. Here are some fascinating facts of the world of English varieties across the continent.

Established English Varieties:
British Isles: the United Kingdom and Ireland have their own well-established Englishes, with distinct accents, vocabulary, and even spelling (think "colour" vs. "color"). Hiberno-English (Ireland) and Scottish English showcase these unique features.
Former British Colonies: Countries like Malta and Cyprus, with a history of British rule, use English as an official language, often influenced by British-English conventions.

Euro English:
A Blend of Influences: this emerging variety, used in the European Union (EU) context, reflects the multilingual nature of the EU. It incorporates elements of British English, technical terms, and influences from the native languages of its speakers.
• Unique Features: Euro English might use calques (direct translations from other languages), have specific vocabulary related to EU functions, and exhibit slightly different grammar structures.

Learning and Using English in Europe:
• Education: English is a required subject in most European schools, with a focus on standard British or American English for communication.
• Communication: English serves as a lingua franca (common language) for Europeans from different countries. This Euro English variety allows for mutual understanding despite national variations.

Multiple Englishes, Shared Benefits:
The presence of various English dialects in Europe reflects the continent's rich linguistic landscape. While there might be slight differences, the score remains the same: English as a tool for communication and understanding across borders.

passage.content:
Hygiene has played a vital role in human civilization throughout history.
Ancient civilizations, such as the Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans, were among the first to recognize the importance of cleanliness for health.
They practiced bathing and used natural oils to maintain personal hygiene.
The Romans even built **elaborate** public bathhouses, which became social centers for relaxation and sanitation.
These early efforts showed an understanding that hygiene was linked to overall well-being.

During the Middle Ages, however, attitudes towards hygiene changed significantly.
The spread of diseases like the Black Death led people to believe that bathing could make **them** more vulnerable to infections.
As a result, frequent bathing became rare, and cleanliness was not prioritized.
Many people relied on strong perfumes to cover body odor, while poor waste management in cities created **unsanitary** conditions.
This lack of hygiene contributed to widespread illness and high mortality rates.

The 19th century marked a turning point in the understanding of hygiene with the rise of scientific discoveries.
Pioneers like Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister demonstrated the link between germs and diseases, leading to improved medical practices and public health measures.
**The introduction of handwashing and sterilization in hospitals greatly reduced infection rates.**
Public awareness campaigns and government regulations began to promote better hygiene in everyday life.

Today, hygiene remains a crucial aspect of public health and daily routines.
Advancements in technology have made access to clean water and sanitation facilities more widespread.
People now understand the importance of practices like handwashing, brushing teeth, and proper waste disposal.
The history of hygiene reflects humanity's ongoing efforts to protect health and prevent disease, proving its significance across time.

passage.content:
[I] Stress has become a significant problem for many students in today’s educational environment.
[II] Many students feel stressed because of heavy workloads, tough exams, and the high expectations set by parents and teachers.
[III] This stress can impact both their mental and physical health, making it challenging to concentrate and perform well academically.
[IV]

One of the primary causes of stress at school is the intense pressure to succeed.
Students are frequently expected to **excel** in all subjects, participate in extracurricular activities, and complete assignments on time.
The fear that **they** might fail or not meet expectations can lead to self-doubt and anxiety.
Moreover, the competition for top grades and college admissions has increased, adding even more pressure.
This kind of stress can cause students to feel overwhelmed, especially when they struggle to balance their studies with other aspects of their lives.

Another contributing factor to school stress is social pressure. Many students face challenges such as bullying, peer pressure, or the need to fit in with their classmates.
These social issues can make school a stressful place, causing students to feel isolated or excluded.
Additionally, the widespread use of social media has created new sources of stress, as students often compare their lives to the seemingly perfect lives of others online.
This comparison can lead to feelings of **inadequacy** and low self-esteem, further increasing their stress levels.

There are several effective ways to help students manage stress at school.
**Providing access to mental health resources, such as counseling services, can offer students a safe space to express their concerns.**
Schools can also organize stress management workshops that teach relaxation techniques, such as deep breathing and meditation.
Encouraging students to practice good time management and get enough sleep can improve their ability to handle stress.
Finally, support from teachers and parents, who emphasize the importance of effort over perfection, can make a significant difference in reducing stress.

In the good old days of school, life was simpler and filled with happiness. Can you imagine a time without smartphones or computers? Instead, we spent our days outside, playing games like hopscotch and tag with our friends.

Our school was a small building with chalkboards and colourful posters. Our teachers were kind and patient, guiding us through the wonders of education using books and paper. During recess, we played fun games and the air was filled with laughter and joy.

Our lunches were packed in lunch boxes with tasty sandwiches and fresh fruit. When the school bell rang, we eagerly ran outside to enjoy the fresh air. Homework was done with pencils and erasers, and we took our time to complete it. Our backpacks were filled with textbooks and notebooks, and we proudly carried them home every day. The best part of the week was receiving gold stars as a reward for good behaviour and hard work.

Thinking back on those school days always brings a smile to my face. They were special times of innocence and discovery, where the world seemed vast and our dreams had no limits.

passage.content:
New Zealand, a stunning island nation in the southwestern Pacific Ocean, is famous for its breathtaking natural wonders and unique biodiversity. It consists of two main landmasses the North Island and the South Island-along with numerous smaller islands.

One of the most remarkable features of New Zealand is its diverse landscape. On the North Island, visitors can explore active volcanic zones, geothermal wonders like Rotorua, and beautiful golden beaches. In contrast, the South Island is home to the majestic Southern Alps, dramatic fjords like Milford Sound, and massive glaciers.

The country is also well-known for its unique wildlife. Because New Zealand was isolated for millions of years, many of its plants and animals are found nowhere else on Earth. The most famous is the kiwi, a flightless bird that has become a national symbol.

English is the **predominant** language spoken in New Zealand, but it has a unique local flavor known as "New Zealand English" or "Kiwi English." It is influenced by Māori, the language of the indigenous people. For example, many place names and common expressions come from Māori culture.

Today, New Zealand is a popular destination for eco-tourism. The government and local communities work hard to protect their natural heritage, ensuring that future generations can enjoy the "pure" beauty of their islands.

passage.content:
In an era dominated by digital interfaces, traditional libraries stand as bastions of tactile knowledge acquisition. These repositories of printed wisdom offer a multisensory experience that digital alternatives often fail to replicate. While e-readers and online databases have revolutionized information accessibility, the physical library continues to assert **its** relevance through unique attributes that resonate with scholars and casual readers alike.

The deliberate atmosphere of libraries—characterized by hushed conversations and the subtle scent of aged paper—fosters contemplation in ways that digital environments rarely achieve. The tangible interaction with books engenders cognitive benefits that transcend mere information transfer. Research indicates that spatial memory activates more robustly when readers navigate physical pages rather than scrolling through digital text. This embodied cognition enhances comprehension and **retention**, particularly for complex material. Furthermore, the serendipitous discoveries that occur while browsing shelves—stumbling upon adjacent volumes that unexpectedly illuminate one's research—represent an algorithmic unpredictability that digital recommendation systems strive to emulate but seldom match. The sensation of weight, texture, and dimension of books provides contextual cues that augment the reading experience.

Libraries face unprecedented challenges as digital resources proliferate. Declining **patronage** and budget constraints have compelled many institutions to reconsider their operational models. This existential dilemma has prompted librarians to advocate for their spaces as more than mere book warehouses. The misconception that libraries have become obsolete underestimates their evolving social function. Moreover, the digital divide remains a significant barrier, with libraries serving as crucial access points for those without reliable internet connections or technological resources.

The contemporary library increasingly functions as a hybrid knowledge ecosystem. Forward-thinking institutions have incorporated makerspaces, digital labs, and community gathering areas alongside traditional collections. __This transformation reflects a nuanced understanding that libraries serve not only as repositories of information but also as catalysts for knowledge creation and community engagement.__ Rather than diminishing the library's significance, technology has prompted its reinvention as an innovative nexus where digital and physical resources converge. Libraries thus persist not as anachronisms but as adaptive cultural institutions meeting diverse intellectual needs.

passage.content:
In recent years, a remarkable revival of traditional apprenticeships has emerged across industries that once **rode roughshod over** hands-on training in favor of academic credentials. This renaissance reflects a growing recognition that theoretical knowledge alone cannot substitute for practical expertise developed through mentorship and real-world application. As automation transforms workplaces, employers increasingly value the human element—craftsmanship, problem-solving, and interpersonal skills that apprenticeships cultivate.
[I] These timeless learning methods now address contemporary challenges, bridging generational knowledge gaps while meeting urgent workforce demands.

Economic factors have significantly accelerated this resurgence. With university tuition reaching prohibitive levels and graduate employment uncertain, many young people seek alternative pathways to professional success. Apprenticeships offer a compelling proposition: earn while you learn, develop marketable skills, and avoid crippling debt.
[II] Industries facing critical shortages—from advanced manufacturing to cybersecurity—have established robust apprenticeship programs to cultivate talent **pipelines**. These initiatives create symbiotic relationships: businesses secure qualified workers while apprentices gain specialized expertise and professional networks, fostering sustainable workforce development ecosystems.

The apprenticeship model delivers benefits beyond financial considerations. Through immersive learning experiences, apprentices develop comprehensive competencies that classroom education cannot replicate. **They** acquire technical proficiency alongside crucial soft skills like adaptability, communication, and critical thinking.
[III] Research consistently shows higher retention rates among workers who complete apprenticeships, resulting in more stable employment relationships. Perhaps most significantly, this model preserves and transmits specialized techniques through direct mentorship, safeguarding cultural and industrial heritage that might otherwise vanish in our digital age.

[IV] Virtual reality now enables apprentices to practice hazardous procedures within safe yet realistic environments, while blockchain-based credentials secure skills recognition with a level of transparency never seen before. __Progressive programs increasingly integrate entrepreneurship, preparing individuals not only for stable employment but also for innovation, self-direction, and the creation of new enterprises.__ At the same time, as climate challenges reshape every sector, green apprenticeships are emerging to cultivate ecological expertise and sustainable practices. This evolving landscape represents not a nostalgic return to outdated models but a forward-looking synthesis—preserving the enduring principles of experiential learning while embracing transformative technologies to forge adaptable, resilient workforces prepared for an uncertain future.

passage.content:
Gender inequality in healthcare remains a persistent global challenge. Women and men often receive different levels of medical attention and treatment quality, creating disparities that affect overall public health outcomes. These inequalities are not merely social issues but **constitute** significant public health concerns that require comprehensive solutions. Medical institutions worldwide are gradually acknowledging that gender-equitable healthcare is essential for achieving optimal population health.

Research consistently demonstrates that women frequently encounter obstacles when seeking medical care. They often face dismissal of **their** symptoms, particularly for conditions like chronic pain, which medical professionals may trivialize compared to identical symptoms in male patients. Additionally, women from marginalized communities experience compounded difficulties, as intersecting factors like race and socioeconomic status exacerbate these disparities. This systemic neglect can lead to delayed diagnoses and inadequate treatment protocols, undermining women's overall well-being.

The roots of healthcare disparities lie in deep-seated societal biases and structural inadequacies. Historical medical research **predominantly** focused on male subjects, resulting in treatment guidelines that may not be optimally effective for women. Economic factors also contribute significantly, as women globally tend to have lower incomes and less comprehensive insurance coverage, limiting their access to specialized care. These barriers are particularly pronounced in developing regions, where cultural norms may further impede women's autonomy in health decision-making.

Addressing gender disparities requires multifaceted interventions at various levels. __Healthcare providers must receive training to recognize and mitigate unconscious biases that influence clinical decisions.__ Policy reforms are essential to ensure equitable insurance coverage and accessibility regardless of gender. Furthermore, medical research must prioritize gender diversity in clinical trials to develop more effective treatments for all patients. By elevating gender equality to a central public health priority, societies can work toward eliminating these harmful disparities and improving health outcomes for everyone.

passage.content:
In recent years, the concept of allyship has gained significant attention in social justice movements. Many people express solidarity with marginalized groups, yet their support often remains superficial. [I] Real commitment demands consistent action in both public and private spheres. Whether someone merely posts on social media or attends occasional protests is **neither here nor there** if they don't challenge fundamental power structures. True progress requires moving beyond passive allyship toward becoming active co-creators of equality, working alongside marginalized communities rather than simply speaking for them.

Conventional allyship frequently falls short of creating lasting change. [II] The performative nature of such activism often masks underlying resistance to change. Such limited involvement often perpetuates existing power dynamics, with privileged supporters maintaining **their** comfort while marginalized individuals continue bearing the burden of educating and organizing. Additionally, many allies retreat when facing criticism or when advocacy becomes inconvenient, demonstrating that temporary support differs significantly from committed co-creation.

Becoming a co-creator of equality demands deeper engagement. Co-creators recognize that equality benefits everyone, not just marginalized groups. Their work often requires personal sacrifice and confronting uncomfortable truths daily. They consistently examine their privileges, amplify underrepresented voices, and share resources without seeking recognition. Unlike passive allies who wait for instructions, co-creators proactively identify opportunities to challenge discrimination in their **spheres** of influence. [III] This approach transforms supportive bystanders into genuine partners who share responsibility for dismantling barriers and rebuilding more equitable systems.

The transition from allyship to co-creation represents a crucial evolution in social justice work. __While allies stand alongside marginalized communities, co-creators work with them to reimagine and rebuild social structures.__ This transformation enables sustainable change where traditional approaches have repeatedly failed. This shift requires humility, consistent self-education, and a willingness to make mistakes while learning. By embracing co-creation, we acknowledge that equality cannot be granted by benevolent supporters but must be constructed collaboratively by diverse participants. [IV] The future of social justice depends not on having more allies, but on cultivating more co-creators committed to collective liberation.

Vietnam has embraced pharmaceutical partnerships as a cornerstone of healthcare development over the past decade.  Following the 2018 regulatory reforms, the nation has attracted fifteen major international pharmaceutical companies seeking to establish local production facilities.  These collaborations have facilitated knowledge transfer, enabling Vietnamese manufacturers to enhance product quality while maintaining competitive pricing.  Domestic pharmaceutical production now accounts for approximately 45% of the national market, reflecting **substantial** growth from just 30% five years ago.

Digital innovation has transformed medication distribution throughout Vietnam's diverse regions.  Mobile applications connecting patients to pharmaceutical suppliers have revolutionized **their** access to medication, particularly in rural areas where traditional pharmacies are scarce.  This technological integration faces challenges, including digital literacy barriers among older populations and internet connectivity issues in remote provinces.  Nevertheless, digital pharmaceutical platforms have experienced 25% annual growth, demonstrating strong consumer adoption despite these obstacles.

Vietnam has prioritized developing domestic production capabilities for essential medicines previously imported at high costs.  Local manufacturers now produce over 150 generic medications, significantly reducing **dependency** on foreign supplies during global disruptions.  Universities have established specialized pharmaceutical programs in partnership with industry leaders, addressing the critical need for skilled professionals.  However, advanced treatments and specialized pharmaceuticals remain predominantly imported, highlighting areas requiring further development.

Environmental considerations have become increasingly important in Vietnam's pharmaceutical partnerships.  **New regulations require manufacturing facilities to implement eco-friendly practices, with particular emphasis on water conservation and waste reduction.**  Several companies have pioneered biodegradable packaging, setting new standards for the industry.  These sustainability initiatives align with international best practices while enhancing the appeal of Vietnamese pharmaceutical products in global markets where environmental consciousness continues to grow.

sections.name: Reading Comprehension

passage.content:
The debate over how gender norms develop has long fascinated researchers and the general public alike.  While some believe our gender behaviors are primarily biological, others argue they're shaped by social experiences and cultural expectations.  **Off the record**, many scientists admit this topic remains controversial because truly definitive studies are difficult to design and interpret objectively.  [I] The nature versus nurture question continues to drive research into how children develop gendered behaviors and whether these patterns are inevitable or malleable through different parenting approaches.

Biological factors undoubtedly contribute to gender development in meaningful ways.  Studies of hormonal influences show that prenatal testosterone exposure affects brain development and subsequent behavior.  [II] For instance, studies have found that male **infants** tend to look longer at mechanical objects, while females often show greater interest in faces and social stimuli.  These findings suggest some gender differences may have biological foundations that influence development from early stages.

Environmental influences also play a crucial role in shaping gender identity and expression.  Parents, peers, media, and educational institutions all transmit messages about "appropriate" gender behavior.  Children observe and internalize these cues from an early age.  Studies show that adults interact differently with babies based on perceived gender, speaking more gently to those **they** believe are girls and engaging in more physical play with presumed boys.  [III] This differential treatment reinforces certain behavioral patterns and expectations throughout childhood.

The evidence points toward an integrated understanding where biology and environment interact continuously throughout development.  [IV] Neither nature nor nurture alone fully explains gender development.  **Instead, biological predispositions create tendencies that environmental factors can either reinforce or modify over time.**  As our understanding evolves, we recognize that gender expression exists on a spectrum rather than in rigid categories.  Moving forward, research that acknowledges this complex interplay will likely provide the most comprehensive insights into gender socialization processes and outcomes.

passage.content:
For hundreds of years, one remote hill in the middle of England has hosted one of the weirdest and most hazardous festivals in the world. It’s the Cooper’s Hill Cheese Rolling Festival. The event is held every year at the end of May. Some people believe that the festival originated from a tradition of rolling burning bundles of sticks down the hill to celebrate the end of winter.

Today, the festival has grown into an international event, with over 15,000 participants and spectators from all over the world joining each year. The rules are simple. A large wheel of cheese is rolled down the hill, and participants chase after it. The first runner to make it to the bottom of the hill is the winner. The winner of the race is allowed to keep the cheese as a prize.

Cooper’s Hill is only 200 meters long, but it is very steep. As a result, racers do not run down the hill; instead, they usually fall down the hill head over heels. This has led to a lot of accidents. For this reason, the event was officially canceled in 2010. Outraged fans have continued the event unofficially since then.

These days, if you want to travel from New York to Beijing, the flight takes about 16 hours. You also have to wait at the airport, and sometimes you have to transfer onto a different airplane. If you add all of that extra time, the trip takes at least 20 hours.

But in the **future**, the trip from New York to Beijing might only take two hours. Right now, a private company is developing something called ET3. ET3 stands for “evacuated tube transport technology”. The capsules use electricity instead of gasoline. For international travel, the capsules can travel at about 6,500 kilometers per hour. That is much faster than airplane - most modern airplanes usually only fly at about 800 kilometers per hour.

There are other **advantages** to ET3. Because it uses electricity, it is quite clean. In addition, it is much quieter than airplanes and cars. Finally, ET3 tubes and capsules don’t require very much building material.

sections.name: Reading Comprehension

passage.content:
Traveling responsibly means exploring new destinations while contributing positively to local environments. Conservation projects worldwide offer tourists opportunities to protect endangered species, restore habitats, and preserve cultural heritage. These initiatives depend on visitor participation and financial support to achieve **their** missions. By integrating conservation activities into your journey, you transform an ordinary vacation into a meaningful experience that benefits wildlife and communities facing environmental challenges.

Research represents the initial step when planning conservation-oriented travel. Identify legitimate organizations operating in your destination through environmental certification websites or tourism boards. Many **reputable** projects welcome volunteers for activities ranging from beach cleanups to wildlife monitoring. Financial contributions directly fund essential equipment, educational programs, and staff salaries. Additionally, some hotels and tour operators donate percentages of their profits to nearby conservation efforts, so selecting these businesses amplifies your impact without requiring extra time.

sections.name: Reading Comprehension

passage.content:
John Muir, celebrated as the "Father of National Parks," pioneered conservation efforts in the late 19th century. During his wilderness expeditions, he would often **sleep like a log** beneath towering sequoias after lengthy hikes documenting flora and fauna. His passionate advocacy captured President Theodore Roosevelt's imagination, resulting in America's first protected territories. [I] Their collaboration established fundamental principles for environmental stewardship that would transform humanity's relationship with natural spaces, creating a legacy that extends far beyond their lifetimes.

The mid-20th century witnessed conservation's evolution from isolated preservation to systematic policy. Rachel Carson's revolutionary work "Silent Spring" (1962) unveiled pesticide dangers, awakening public consciousness about ecological fragility. [II] The inaugural Earth Day celebration mobilized unprecedented numbers, generating momentum for crucial legislation, including the Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Protection measures, which continue to safeguard **our** ecosystems despite industrial opposition and political fluctuations.

Today's conservation landscape encompasses diverse approaches addressing multifaceted challenges. Indigenous communities increasingly lead initiatives blending ancestral wisdom with contemporary scientific methodology. [III] Digital innovations enable real-time monitoring of threatened species across remote habitats. Meanwhile, youth-driven climate movements demonstrate remarkable resilience, challenging corporate practices and governmental **inaction**. Modern conservation has expanded beyond wilderness defense to incorporate sustainable agriculture, environmental justice, and carbon-neutral development strategies.

The movement's future appears radically different from its origins, yet it maintains Muir's fundamental vision. __While accelerating habitat destruction and climate disruption pose existential threats, emergent solutions offer promising alternatives.__ Regenerative economics challenges traditional growth models, while restoration ecology demonstrates nature's remarkable resilience when given the opportunity. Urban conservation initiatives transform concrete landscapes into wildlife corridors, reconnecting fragmented habitats. Digital platforms democratize participation, allowing citizens worldwide to contribute meaningful data. [IV] Conservation's next century will likely witness unprecedented collaboration between artificial intelligence, indigenous knowledge, and community stewardship—reimagining humanity not as nature's conqueror but as its conscientious guardian.

passage.content:
The Maker Movement represents a revolutionary approach to education that emphasizes learning through creating, building, and experimenting. This educational philosophy, developed from Papert's theory of constructionism, encourages students to construct knowledge through hands-on projects rather than passive consumption of information. The movement has gained momentum in educational institutions worldwide, transforming traditional classrooms into collaborative workshops where innovation thrives. If schools fully embraced the Maker Movement, (18)______. This pedagogical shift promotes the acquisition of valuable competencies such as problem-solving, perseverance, and adaptability that are essential in our rapidly evolving digital landscape. The Maker Movement, (19)______, has now infiltrated formal education systems from primary schools to universities. Digital fabrication tools like 3D printers and laser cutters, once accessible only to specialized industries, have become integral components of modern maker spaces where learners engage in authentic design challenges.

Constructionism builds on constructivist theory; (20)______. Many educators advocate for this experiential approach to learning, yet implementation obstacles persist in conventional educational frameworks that prioritize standardized assessment. (21)______, which constitutes the core principle of the Maker Movement, has transformed instructional methodologies across diverse disciplines. Through iteration and prototyping, students discover that failure represents an opportunity for growth rather than a final outcome. Impressive outcomes have been documented by educational researchers when maker-centered learning is incorporated in curricula, (22)______. The maker mindset cultivates not only technical abilities but also fosters creativity and collaborative skills essential for future success.

sections.instructionText: Read the following passage about How Ecotourism Empowers Women in Local Communities and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 23 to 30.
sections.name: Reading Comprehension

passage.content:
Ecotourism has emerged as a powerful catalyst for gender equality in rural and indigenous communities worldwide. Unlike conventional tourism that often overlooks local participation, sustainable travel initiatives **deliberately** integrate women into various aspects of the tourism value chain. These environmentally conscious ventures provide visitors with authentic cultural experiences while simultaneously creating pathways for female economic independence. Organizations promoting responsible tourism increasingly recognize women as essential stakeholders whose traditional knowledge about local ecosystems and cultural heritage represents invaluable assets for conservation efforts.

The financial impact of ecotourism on women's livelihoods manifests through diverse entrepreneurial opportunities. In coastal regions of Southeast Asia, women establish successful homestay operations, craft businesses, and create culinary tours showcasing traditional cooking methods. These enterprises generate steady income streams that women typically reinvest in **their** families' education and healthcare. Research indicates that female-operated ecotourism ventures demonstrate remarkable resilience during economic downturns compared to other sectors, partly because they often build upon existing skills rather than requiring entirely new competencies.

Beyond economic advantages, ecotourism nurtures women's professional development through skill acquisition and leadership roles. Educational workshops on business management, conservation techniques, and foreign languages enhance women's capabilities and confidence. In several African communities, women previously restricted to domestic responsibilities now serve as tour guides, conservation officers, and **hospitality** managers. This transformation challenges entrenched gender norms and gradually reshapes perceptions about women's capabilities. Importantly, when mothers achieve financial independence, they become powerful role models for younger generations.

Despite promising progress, obstacles persist in maximizing ecotourism's empowerment potential for women. Cultural barriers occasionally limit female participation in certain tourism activities, while insufficient access to credit hampers business expansion. __Additionally, unequal property rights in some regions prevent women from fully capitalizing on land-based ecotourism opportunities.__ Nevertheless, forward-thinking policies promoting women's involvement in decision-making processes, along with targeted training programs addressing gender-specific challenges, continue to dismantle these barriers. The future of sustainable tourism increasingly depends on women's contributions to conservation and community development.

sections.name: Reading Comprehension

passage.content:
Intuitive learning represents a fascinating dimension of human cognition where knowledge acquisition occurs beneath conscious awareness. [I] Unlike traditional structured learning, intuitive processes operate silently in the background as our brains absorb patterns and connections without deliberate effort. Many educational innovators have begun to **get in on the act**, incorporating techniques that stimulate these natural learning mechanisms. This approach acknowledges that formal instruction captures only a fraction of our learning potential, while unconscious processing continuously interprets environmental cues. Scientific evidence increasingly validates the significance of intuition in knowledge development, suggesting that our brains process substantially more information than we consciously recognize.

[II] When students encounter complex problems, **their** minds activate implicit memory systems that draw upon previously absorbed patterns. This recognition occurs before conscious awareness engages, explaining why solutions sometimes appear suddenly after periods of mental incubation. Neuroscientists have documented increased activity in specific brain regions during these "Aha!" moments, when seemingly disconnected information spontaneously reorganizes into meaningful structures. The phenomenon resembles assembling a puzzle without deliberately examining each piece-connections emerge naturally when the mind remains receptive.

Integrating intuitive approaches into educational frameworks yields remarkable benefits for learners across disciplines. Students develop heightened pattern recognition capabilities that transfer between subject areas, enhancing their problem-solving versatility. [III] Furthermore, intuitive learning fosters deeper engagement with material as learners develop genuine curiosity rather than merely memorizing facts. This authentic connection with knowledge promotes exceptional **retention** rates compared with purely analytical approaches. Perhaps most significantly, cultivating intuition builds resilience against cognitive overload in our information-saturated environment, as unconscious processing efficiently filters and prioritizes incoming data without taxing conscious attention.

Educational applications of intuitive learning principles continue expanding across diverse contexts. Teachers implementing project-based explorations observe students naturally discovering mathematical concepts through physical manipulation before formal explanations. [IV] Language acquisition programs utilizing immersive environments demonstrate superior results compared to traditional vocabulary memorization. __Corporate training increasingly incorporates simulations where participants internalize complex decision-making frameworks through repeated exposure rather than explicit instruction.__ As research advances our understanding of unconscious cognitive mechanisms, educational methodologies will likely evolve to harness these powerful intuitive capacities more effectively, fundamentally transforming how knowledge transfer occurs.

passage.content:
Sustainable tourism has emerged as a vital approach for travelers seeking to minimize their environmental footprint while enjoying meaningful experiences. Eco-friendly adventures focus on conserving natural resources and respecting local communities. Unlike conventional tourism, which often prioritizes convenience over conservation, green travel encourages mindful choices. This movement has gained traction among younger generations who scrutinize the ecological impact of **their** vacation decisions, representing a shift from mere leisure to environmental stewardship.

Transportation typically accounts for the largest carbon **expenditure** in travel. Opting for trains rather than flights can substantially reduce emissions, while utilizing public transport at your destination further diminishes impact. When selecting accommodation, look for establishments with recognized sustainability certifications. Genuine eco-lodges often harness renewable energy, implement water conservation, and source provisions locally. These facilities usually integrate with their surroundings, using designs that minimize disruption to habitats while maximizing energy efficiency.

Responsible activities **constitute** another crucial element of sustainable travel. Instead of attractions that exploit wildlife, travelers should seek experiences fostering genuine connections with nature. Bird-watching, guided hikes, and conservation projects offer enriching alternatives to tourist traps. Purchasing crafts directly from local artisans provides authentic souvenirs while supporting indigenous economies. When exploring wilderness areas, adhere to established trails and follow "leave no trace" principles by removing all waste.

The benefits of eco-friendly travel extend beyond environmental preservation. Sustainable practices frequently deliver more authentic cultural exchanges and deeper connections with destinations. By engaging respectfully with local communities, travelers foster mutual understanding. __Moreover, eco-adventures often create more meaningful personal experiences by promoting mindfulness.__ Many travelers report that sustainable journeys yield more vivid memories than conventional vacations, proving that eco-friendly adventures enhance rather than diminish the travel experience.

Our oceans cover over 70% of Earth's surface and contain 97% of our planet's water, making them essential for all life. Nations that prioritize marine protection can **walk tall** in global environmental forums, as ocean health directly influences climate stability, food security, and economic prosperity. The Blue [I] Revolution represents a fundamental shift in how humanity approaches ocean management, transitioning from exploitation to stewardship. Unlike previous environmental movements focused primarily on terrestrial concerns, this revolution acknowledges that our future prosperity hinges on maintaining thriving marine ecosystems.

Marine environments face unprecedented challenges from multiple fronts. Rising sea temperatures have triggered catastrophic coral bleaching, destroying habitats that support a quarter of all marine species. [II] Overfishing continues to deplete populations of keystone species, creating cascading effects throughout food webs. Additionally, ocean acidification-caused by **our** excessive carbon dioxide emissions-threatens to dissolve the calcium carbonate structures of shellfish and coral reefs, fundamentally altering marine chemistry and biology.

Innovative conservation approaches offer promising solutions to these complex challenges. Marine protected areas (MPAs) have demonstrated remarkable success in **rejuvenating** fish populations and restoring ecosystem resilience. Sustainable fishing practices, including catch limits and selective gear requirements, help maintain fish stocks while supporting coastal livelihoods. Technological breakthroughs in ocean cleanup systems now allow efficient removal of floating plastic debris. [III] Furthermore, seaweed farming and coral restoration projects actively rebuild critical habitats while sequestering carbon. These diverse strategies demonstrate that environmental protection and economic vitality can advance together harmoniously.

The next decade represents a critical window for implementing these solutions at scale. [IV] Expanding protected ocean territory to 30% by 2030 would safeguard biodiversity hotspots while enhancing fishery productivity in surrounding waters. __International cooperation on plastic reduction and carbon emissions will determine whether coral reefs survive beyond this century.__ By embracing the Blue Revolution's principles, we can ensure that future generations inherit oceans teeming with life rather than depleted marine deserts. Our collective choices today will echo through ocean ecosystems for centuries to come.
